title: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
summary: How three production allocators turn size classes and caches into fast, scalable malloc: jemalloc's arenas and bitmap slabs, mimalloc's sharded per-page free lists, tcmalloc's rseq per-CPU caches and hugepage-aware heap.
outcomes: Map jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc onto one skeleton: size classes, local cache, shared middle, page back-end
Compute size-class rounding waste and jemalloc slab sizes for a given request size
Trace mimalloc's free, local_free and thread_free lists through local and cross-thread frees
Explain how tcmalloc's per-CPU caches commit with rseq and how Temeraire places requests in hugepages
Choose allocator settings (arenas, cache mode, purge delay) for a memory or tail-latency goal

lessons.title: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches

blocks.md: A general-purpose `malloc` has to serve requests from 8 bytes to gigabytes, from one thread or hundreds, and it never knows what the program will do next. Three open-source allocators are common drop-in replacements for the C library's: **jemalloc**, **mimalloc** (from Microsoft Research) and **tcmalloc** (from Google). Linking one in changes nothing in your code, yet it can change throughput, tail latency and resident memory.

From the prerequisites you already know the two forces they balance. A **thread cache** (or magazine) lets most calls skip shared, locked state, but every cached object is memory nobody is using. **Fragmentation** is memory the allocator holds but cannot use for the request at hand: *internal* (rounding a request up) and *external* (free space split into unusable pieces).

This course shows that the three allocators share one skeleton and differ in a few precise decisions. Learn the skeleton first and each allocator becomes a short list of differences.

blocks.title: The shared skeleton, and what each allocator calls its layers

scenes.caption: Four layers sit between your call and the kernel. Each layer is slower and more shared than the one to its left, and each one exists to make the layer to its left rarer.
The common case: round the size to a class, pop a cached object from the local cache, return. No lock, no atomic read-modify-write, a handful of instructions.
A miss moves a whole batch from the shared middle, which may carve new pages from the back-end, which may ask the OS. Freeing runs the same path in reverse when a cache overflows.
jemalloc: a per-thread tcache in front of one of many arenas; each arena has a locked bin per size class and manages page extents, purging unused pages on a timer.
mimalloc: no separate cache layer. Each thread owns pages, and each page keeps its own free lists; other threads hand objects back with one atomic push.

labels.loc:
page free list
owned by thread

scenes.caption: tcmalloc: a per-CPU (or legacy per-thread) cache, a middle-end of transfer cache plus central free list per size class, and a hugepage-aware page heap.

blocks.md:
**Size classes** come first. Instead of tracking every possible size, the allocator keeps a fixed menu and rounds each request up to the next entry. Objects of one class can be packed side by side in a run of pages, so the allocator needs no per-object header to know an object's size: the size is a property of the page or span the object sits in.

jemalloc's manual states its rule (64-bit, 4 KiB pages, 16-byte quantum): tiny class 8, then multiples of 16 up to 128, then **four classes per doubling**: 160, 192, 224, 256, then 320, 384, 448, 512, and so on. mimalloc's bins follow the same four-per-doubling shape in machine words. tcmalloc instead uses a hand-tuned table chosen to minimize measured waste, so its spacing is irregular (for example 144, 176, 208, then later 3456, 4096, 4736).

blocks.caption: With four classes per doubling, the classes above a power of two b are spaced d = b/4 apart. A request just above b rounds up by almost d, so the worst internal waste approaches 20 percent, matching jemalloc's manual.

blocks.title: Bytes wasted by rounding the same request

scenes.caption: malloc(200): jemalloc and mimalloc round to 224 (24 B wasted, 10.7 percent). tcmalloc has a 208-byte class, so it wastes only 8 B.
malloc(520): 640 for jemalloc and mimalloc (120 B, 18.8 percent, close to the 20 percent bound). tcmalloc's table has 576, wasting 56 B.
malloc(3000): now the irregular table loses. jemalloc and mimalloc have 3072 (72 B); tcmalloc's next class is 3456, wasting 456 B (13.2 percent).
malloc(4100): just past 4096, the worst spot for regular spacing. jemalloc and mimalloc jump to 5120 (1020 B, 19.9 percent); tcmalloc's 4736 wastes 636 B.

blocks.md: Numbers above assume x86-64 defaults: jemalloc with 4 KiB pages and a 16-byte quantum, tcmalloc's default 16-byte-aligned table for its default 8 KiB pages, and a release build of mimalloc. Other builds use other tables.

blocks.prompt: A request for 24 bytes: mimalloc counts sizes in 8-byte words, so 24 bytes is exactly 3 words. Does mimalloc hand back a 24-byte block?
blocks.reveal: No, it hands back 32 bytes, like the other two. `malloc` must return memory aligned for any type, which is 16 bytes on x86-64. mimalloc's bin function rounds sizes of up to 8 words to an even number of words when the maximum alignment is two words, so 3 words become 4. All three allocators waste 8 bytes here (25 percent): small requests pay the most for alignment.

blocks.md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

blocks.question: Why can a size-class allocator answer free(p) without a header word in front of each object?
options: The C standard requires callers to pass the size to free
All objects in one page or span share a size class, so the allocator finds the page's metadata from the address and reads the class there
The allocator scans its free lists until it finds the neighbour of p
Each object stores its size in its last 8 bytes
blocks.explain: Segregating by size means size is a property of the container. jemalloc looks up the extent for the address, tcmalloc consults its pagemap radix tree, and mimalloc computes the page from the address. C's free does not take a size (C++ sized delete can pass one as an optimization).

blocks.question: A service mostly allocates 4,100-byte buffers. Which statement is right?
options: Rounding waste is under 1 percent with any of the three allocators
tcmalloc wastes the most because its classes are irregular
Size classes only affect objects smaller than 1 KiB
jemalloc and mimalloc round to 5,120 and waste about 20 percent; tcmalloc's default table rounds to 4,736
blocks.explain: 4,100 is just above 4,096, the worst spot for four-classes-per-doubling spacing: the next class is 5,120. tcmalloc's tuned table happens to have 4,736 (636 bytes wasted). Irregular tables win or lose depending on the size; at 3,000 bytes tcmalloc was the worst.

lessons.title: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging

blocks.md:
jemalloc attacks lock contention with **arenas**: independent allocators, each with its own locks, bins and pages. A thread is bound to one arena, so threads on different arenas never contend. The default maximum, `opt.narenas`, is **four times the number of CPUs** (one if there is a single CPU): a 16-CPU machine gets up to 64 arenas.

Which arena does a new thread get? In the source (`arena_choose_hard`), a thread's first allocation scans the arenas: if one has no threads it takes it, if an uninitialized slot remains it creates a new arena there, and once all exist it picks the first arena with the fewest bound threads.

blocks.title: Binding threads to arenas (toy setting: narenas = 3)

scenes.caption: Arena 0 always exists. The main thread binds to it. Arenas 1 and 2 are slots that have not been created yet.
T1 arrives. Arena 0 already has a thread and slot 1 is empty, so jemalloc creates arena 1 for T1.
T2 gets a brand-new arena 2 the same way. With narenas threads or fewer, every thread has a private arena and no arena lock is ever shared.
T3: all arenas exist and all have 1 thread. The scan keeps the first arena with the strictly lowest count, so T3 shares arena 0.
T4: arena 0 has 2, arena 1 has 1, arena 2 has 1. Arena 1 is the first with the minimum, so T4 joins it. Load stays balanced by thread count, not by bytes.

blocks.md:
Inside an arena, every small size class has a **bin**: a mutex, a current slab and a heap of non-full slabs. In front of the arena each thread has a **tcache** (`opt.tcache`, on by default) holding stacks of cached pointers per size class up to `opt.tcache_max`, **32 KiB** by default. A hit pops a pointer without any lock. A miss takes the bin's lock once and fills a batch; an overflow flushes a batch back.

Small classes (below 4 pages, so up to 14 KiB with 4 KiB pages) live in **slabs**: a page-aligned run of pages split into equal regions, plus a **bitmap** with one bit per region. Larger classes get their own page-aligned **extent** each.

How many pages per slab? jemalloc's size-class generator (`src/sc.c`) picks the **smallest whole number of pages that the region size divides exactly**, so the slab has zero tail waste. That is the least common multiple of the page size and the region size:

blocks.caption: s = 48 gives 12,288 bytes: 3 pages holding 256 regions. s = 80 gives 5 pages, s = 112 gives 7 pages (256 regions each), and s = 2,560 gives 5 pages holding 8 regions.

blocks.title: A 2,560-byte slab: 5 pages, 8 regions, one bitmap

scenes.caption: lcm(4096, 2560) = 20,480 bytes = 5 pages, exactly 8 regions. A 0 bit means the region is free. The slab's metadata lives outside the slab, so all 20,480 bytes are usable.
Three mallocs. Each one finds the first unset bit, sets it and returns slab base + index x 2,560. Regions 0, 1, 2 are now in use.
free(base + 2,560): the offset divided by 2,560 gives index 1, so bit 1 is cleared. A hole now sits in the middle.
The next malloc again takes the first unset bit: index 1. Reusing low addresses first keeps live data packed toward the start of the slab, so the tail is more likely to stay untouched.
When all 8 bits are set the slab is full and leaves the bin. The bin then takes a non-full slab from its heap, which prefers the oldest slab and then the lowest address.

blocks.md:
Objects freed by a *different* thread go into the freeing thread's tcache first. When that tcache flushes, jemalloc groups the pointers by the arena that owns each slab and takes **that** arena's bin lock to clear the bits. So cross-thread frees are cheap per call but eventually touch the owner's locked bin.

Unused pages are returned to the OS gradually. A page that held data and is now unused is **dirty**. After roughly `opt.dirty_decay_ms` (default **10 seconds**) jemalloc purges it to **muzzy** with `MADV_FREE` where supported (the kernel may reclaim it lazily) or straight to **clean**. A second timer, `opt.muzzy_decay_ms`, governs muzzy to clean. Its default is 0, which means muzzy pages are purged at once, so with default settings decayed dirty pages go straight to clean (`MADV_DONTNEED`). The purge rate follows a smooth S-shaped curve so a burst of frees does not become a burst of system calls.

blocks.title: Share of a burst of dirty pages jemalloc still keeps

scenes.caption: Default 10 s: the source weights the backlog of recently dirtied pages by a smootherstep table. Simplified model: 89.6 percent is still kept at 2.5 s, 50 percent at 5 s, 10.4 percent at 7.5 s, none at 10 s.
1 s decay returns memory fast, but a program that frees and reallocates every few seconds now pays page faults to get the same memory back.
30 s decay keeps memory around for bursty workloads. Resident memory stays near the recent peak for half a minute, which looks like a leak on dashboards.

blocks.md: Without `background_thread`, purging runs inside your application threads as they call into jemalloc, which adds to their tail latency, and an inactive application delays purging. jemalloc's tuning guide suggests `background_thread:true` where extra jemalloc-managed threads are acceptable.

blocks.question: Using jemalloc's rule, how big is the slab for the 96-byte class with 4 KiB pages?
options: 3 pages, 128 regions, no waste
1 page, 42 regions, 64 bytes wasted
2 pages, 85 regions
96 pages, 4,096 regions
blocks.explain: lcm(4096, 96) = 12,288 bytes = 3 pages, and 12,288 / 96 = 128 regions exactly. A 1-page slab would leave 4096 - 42 x 96 = 64 bytes unusable; jemalloc avoids that by growing the slab until the region size divides it.

blocks.question: Thread A allocates objects that thread B frees, and the two are bound to different arenas. Where does contention appear?
options: Nowhere, because each thread only ever touches its own arena
On every free, because B must lock A's arena per object
When B's tcache flushes: the batch is grouped by owning arena and B takes A's bin lock, the same lock A takes to refill
Only in the kernel, when pages are purged
blocks.explain: free goes into B's own tcache without a lock, so the per-call cost is low. But the bits live in A's slabs, so the flush must lock A's bin. Batching amortizes that, yet the lock is shared between the producer's refills and the consumer's flushes.

lessons.title: mimalloc: three free lists per page

blocks.md:
mimalloc's starting observation (Leijen, Zorn and de Moura, MSR-TR-2019-18): one free list per size class lets a program's consecutive allocations land all over the heap, which hurts locality. Its fix is **free list sharding**: a free list *per mimalloc page*, where a page holds blocks of one size and is usually **64 KiB** for small objects. malloc keeps allocating inside one page until it is exhausted, so things allocated close in time sit close in memory.

The report says that in the Lean compiler, replacing a single free list with a free list per page alone gave over 25 percent speedups on some benchmarks with a 1 GiB heap.

Each page then shards its free list once more, into **three lists**:

1. `free`: blocks malloc pops from. Only the owning thread touches it.
2. `local_free`: blocks the owning thread frees. They are *not* pushed onto `free`.
3. `thread_free`: blocks other threads free, pushed with an atomic compare-and-swap (CAS).

Pages belong to one thread's heap, so the owner never needs a lock. Splitting off `local_free` looks pointless until you see what it buys: `free` is guaranteed to run empty after a bounded number of allocations, which forces a visit to the slow path on a regular **cadence**.

blocks.title: One mimalloc page with 6 blocks, three free lists

scenes.caption: A fresh page: every block is on free. (Simplified: real small pages hold hundreds or thousands of blocks; 64 KiB of 48-byte blocks is 1,365.)
The owner mallocs 3 times. Each malloc is one load, one null test and one pop from free. b0, b1, b2 are in use.
The owner frees b1. It goes on local_free, not free, with a plain store: no atomics.
Another thread frees b0. It cannot touch the owner's lists, so it pushes b0 onto thread_free with one CAS. Threads freeing into different pages never contend.
Three more mallocs take b3, b4, b5. free is now empty even though two blocks are reusable: they sit on the other lists.
The next malloc finds free empty and takes the slow path: thread_free is swapped out atomically and put in front of local_free, and the combined list becomes free. b0 is returned; b1 waits on free.

blocks.caption: One branch on each fast path. The segment is found by masking the pointer, the page by a shift.

blocks.md:
`free` must find a page's metadata from a bare pointer. In the report's layout (mimalloc v1), pages live in **segments** of 4 MiB aligned to 4 MiB, and the segment header holds the page descriptors. Clearing the low 22 bits of any pointer gives its segment; the offset shifted right by 16 (64 KiB pages) gives the page index.

Worked example: `p = 0x7f3a12c4d3a0`. Masking gives segment `0x7f3a12c00000`; the offset is `0x4d3a0`, and `0x4d3a0 >> 16 = 4`, so `p` is in page 4. Large and huge pages use shift 22, so their index is always 0: one formula with no special case.

Later versions keep the three lists but changed the OS layer: v2 uses 32 MiB segments built from 64 KiB slices, and v3 drops segments for arenas plus a **page map** that maps each arena slice of address space (64 KiB by default) to its page.

blocks.question: The report prints the segment computation as `(uintptr_t)p & ~(4*MB)`. For `p = 0x7f3a12c4d3a0`, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing, it equals 0x7f3a12c00000
It clears only bit 22, giving 0x7f3a1284d3a0, an address in the middle of the segment rather than its start
It clears every bit above bit 22
It rounds p up to the next segment
blocks.explain: ~(4*MB) is all ones except bit 22. Masking with it clears one bit, and p happens to have bit 22 set, so the result is 0x7f3a1284d3a0: not even aligned. The intended mask is ~(4*MB - 1), which clears the low 22 bits and gives 0x7f3a12c00000. Alignment masks are always size minus one.

blocks.md:
The slow path, `malloc_generic`, does all the batched work in one place. It atomically swaps `thread_free` to empty, links those blocks in front of `local_free`, moves the combined list to `free`, frees pages whose blocks are all free, calls an optional deferred-free hook, and if needed takes a fresh page. Because `local_free` guarantees `free` empties regularly, this runs on a predictable cadence even in a loop that frees and reallocates the same block forever. The report's authors use that cadence for deferred reference-count decrements in the Lean and Koka runtimes and as a deterministic heartbeat.

Remote frees are batched for free as well: the owner collects the whole `thread_free` list with a single atomic swap, however many threads pushed onto it.

scenes.caption: Thread A allocates from its own page by popping free. No atomics are involved.
Thread B frees two of those blocks. Each free is a CAS loop on this page's thread_free head, the only contended word, and only for frees into this page.
A's free list runs dry. In the slow path A swaps thread_free to NULL in one atomic step and appends both blocks to free: two remote frees cost A one atomic.

blocks.md: One more case: if a page is **full**, mimalloc moves it to a separate full list so the slow path does not rescan it (the report describes a SPEC gcc run with over 18,000 full pages). A remote free into a full page must then tell the owner the page has space again. mimalloc encodes a small state in the low bits of the `thread_free` pointer; in the delayed state the first remote free goes onto the owning heap's delayed-free list instead, and the state then returns to normal, so only one free per page pays that extra cost.

mimalloc replaces a per-thread cache with ownership: the thread that owns a page allocates and frees into it with plain loads and stores, and everyone else uses a per-page atomic list that the owner drains in batches.

blocks.question: A loop does `p = malloc(48); free(p);` a billion times on one thread. Without `local_free` (frees pushed straight onto `free`), what would mimalloc lose?
options: The guarantee that the slow path runs regularly, so remote frees and deferred work could wait forever
Correctness: blocks would be handed out twice
Locality, because blocks would come from other pages
Nothing; local_free exists only for debugging
blocks.explain: With one list, the same block is pushed and popped forever and free never empties, so malloc_generic never runs. thread_free would never be collected and deferred-free callbacks would never fire. local_free makes free run dry after a bounded number of allocations.

lessons.title: tcmalloc: rseq per-CPU caches, spans and Temeraire

blocks.md:
tcmalloc splits into a **front-end** (a cache with no locks), a **middle-end** that refills it, and a **back-end** (the page heap) that gets memory from the OS. Requests above `kMaxSize`, **256 KiB** in the default build, skip the caches and go straight to the page heap.

The front-end began as per-thread caches, hence the name Thread-Caching Malloc. The design doc explains why it moved to **per-CPU** caches: with per-thread caches, total cached memory grows with the thread count, and modern applications can have very large thread counts. A per-CPU cache bounds caching by the number of logical CPUs instead.

scenes.caption: A thread running on CPU 3 allocates. Its size class's slot array in CPU 3's cache has objects, so one pop finishes the call.
A thread on CPU 7 frees many objects and CPU 7's array overflows. A batch (32 objects for small classes in the default table) moves to the transfer cache under its mutex.
CPU 3 runs dry and takes a batch from the transfer cache: objects freed on CPU 7 flow to CPU 3 without touching spans. That cross-CPU hand-off is where the name comes from.

If the transfer cache is empty, the central free list pulls objects out of spans. Returned objects are mapped to their span through the pagemap; a span whose objects are all back goes to the page heap.
The page heap supplies spans and talks to the OS. In tcmalloc it is the hugepage-aware allocator (Temeraire), covered below.

blocks.md:
How can a per-CPU cache avoid locks when the thread using it can be preempted and another thread scheduled on the same CPU? With Linux **restartable sequences** (rseq). A restartable sequence is a short block of instructions whose only side effect is its **final single store** (the commit). If the kernel preempts, migrates or signals the thread while its instruction pointer is inside the block, it resumes the thread at an abort handler that restarts the block from the top.

In tcmalloc each CPU's slab has a header per size class with `current` and `end` offsets into an array of object pointers. Push writes the pointer into slot `current`, then commits by storing `current + 1`. Pop reads slot `current - 1`, then commits by storing `current - 1`. No atomic instruction is executed on the fast path.

blocks.title: Two threads push onto CPU 3's array; one is preempted mid-sequence

scenes.caption: T1 on CPU 3 frees X: it reads current = 5 and writes X into slot 5. The commit, storing current = 6, has not happened yet.
The kernel preempts T1 inside the sequence. T2 runs on CPU 3, frees Y, reads current = 5, overwrites slot 5 with Y and commits current = 6. X's uncommitted write is simply lost.
When T1 runs again the kernel sends it to the abort handler, which restarts the sequence: re-read current = 6, write X into slot 6, commit 7. Both X and Y are cached, with no lock and no atomic.

blocks.md: A restartable sequence must tolerate running its prefix many times, so everything before the commit must be side-effect free or harmless to repeat. Writing slot 5 twice is harmless here only because nothing reads beyond `current`.

The middle-end manages memory in **spans**: runs of tcmalloc pages (8 KiB by default, unrelated to the hardware page size). A span used for small objects is cut into objects of one class, at most $2^{16}$ of them, so free objects are tracked with 2-byte indices. With 8 KiB spans, the 48-byte class holds 170 objects with 32 bytes left over, and the 80-byte class holds 102.

The **page heap** got a redesign called **Temeraire**, the hugepage-aware allocator (published at OSDI 2021). Its goal is to keep live data packed into as few 2 MiB hugepages as possible, so those stay fully backed and TLB-friendly while completely empty hugepages are returned whole. It has three parts: a **filler** packs sub-hugepage requests into partly used hugepages, a **region** allocator best-fits requests slightly larger than a hugepage (like 2.1 MiB) across hugepage boundaries in large regions, and a **hugepage cache** serves requests of whole hugepages.

The filler's placement rule is the clever part. It orders hugepages first by their **longest free range** (the largest request each could still serve) and allocates from the hugepage with the *smallest* range that still fits, so long free ranges are saved for requests that need them. Among hugepages with equal longest free range it prefers the one with **more allocations**. Its design doc explains why: a hugepage becomes empty only when every allocation on it is freed, and waiting on one allocation is likelier to pay off than waiting on five.

blocks.title: Temeraire's filler choosing a hugepage (8 KiB pages, 256 per hugepage)

scenes.caption: Four partly used hugepages. Each request below is placed against this same snapshot. Simplified: the real filler buckets allocation counts logarithmically and keeps lists plus a bitmap to find the pick quickly.
Request: 1 page. Every hugepage fits it. The smallest longest-free-range is 2 (B and C). B has more allocations, so B is chosen. A's run of 8 and D's run of 40 stay intact.
Request: 6 pages. B and C cannot fit it. A, with a range of 8, is the tightest fit; D's 40-page range is saved for bigger requests.
Request: 30 pages. Only D fits. Had small requests been placed on D earlier, its 40-page run could be broken and a new hugepage would be needed here.

blocks.md: tcmalloc reserves address space in large chunks (typically 1 GiB regions) without backing it, so virtual size (VSS) can be far above resident size (RSS). Limiting a tcmalloc process with a VSS limit such as `ulimit -v` fails long before it actually uses that much memory.

blocks.question: Why can't tcmalloc's per-CPU pop just be an ordinary load and store of `current` without rseq?
options: It could; per-CPU data is never shared
Two threads can run on the same CPU in turn, and a preemption between the read and the store would let both pop the same object
x86 does not allow stores to per-CPU memory
The kernel zeroes per-CPU memory on every context switch
blocks.explain: A CPU is shared over time by many threads. Without rseq, T1 could read current, be preempted, T2 could pop the same slot and commit, and T1 would then return a duplicate. rseq turns preemption into a restart so the read-modify-write behaves atomically for that CPU without a lock or atomic instruction.

blocks.question: Temeraire's filler has hugepage P with a 50-page free range and hugepage Q with a 3-page free range. A 2-page request arrives. Where does it go and why?
options: P, because it has the most free space
A fresh hugepage, to avoid fragmentation
Q, because it is the tightest fit, which keeps P's long range available for large requests
Whichever was used most recently
blocks.explain: The filler allocates from the hugepage with the smallest longest-free-range that fits. Placing small requests on P would break up its 50-page run, and a later large request would then need a new hugepage.

lessons.title: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory

blocks.md: Now compare the three on the patterns that separate them in production. The first is a **producer-consumer** workload: one thread allocates messages and another frees them. Every object crosses threads, so the cheap local paths alone cannot handle it.

blocks.title: Producer allocates, consumer frees: how objects get home

scenes.caption: jemalloc: T2's frees land in T2's tcache. On overflow T2 flushes a batch grouped by owning arena, locking T1's bin; T1 refills from the same locked bin.
tcmalloc: T2's CPU cache overflows into the size class's transfer cache; T1's CPU cache underflows and takes a batch from it. Spans are never touched while objects keep circulating.
mimalloc: each free by T2 is one CAS onto the block's page thread_free list; T1 collects a whole list with one atomic swap in its slow path. Contention is spread over many pages.

blocks.md: The second pattern is **many threads**. Caching memory per thread multiplies by thread count; caching per CPU multiplies by CPU count. tcmalloc's constants make this concrete (default 8 KiB page build): in legacy per-thread mode the total thread-cache budget is 32 MiB, but each thread's cache may grow to at least 512 KiB, so the design doc warns the total can exceed the budget. In per-CPU mode the default per-CPU limit is 1.5 MiB. jemalloc's tcache is also per thread, while mimalloc keeps no separate cache: free blocks stay in the owning thread's pages.

blocks.title: Upper bound on tcmalloc's front-end cached memory

scenes.caption: 16 CPUs: per-CPU mode caps the front-end at 24 MiB however many threads run. Per-thread mode stays at the 32 MiB budget until 64 threads, then grows by 512 KiB per thread: 200 threads allow 100 MiB.
128 CPUs: the per-CPU bound is now 192 MiB, about what 384 threads allow in per-thread mode. On huge machines, idle CPUs' caches are what tcmalloc's background actions release.

blocks.caption: Simplified bound from tcmalloc's constants. The real per-CPU limit is adjusted at runtime, and busy CPUs can borrow capacity from idle ones.

blocks.md:
The third pattern is **returning memory**. All three keep freed pages for a while because faulting them back in costs time, and each exposes the delay:

- jemalloc: `dirty_decay_ms` (10 s default) and `muzzy_decay_ms`, plus `background_thread` to purge without waiting for allocator calls.
- mimalloc: `MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY`, 1000 ms by default in v3. Purging decommits with `MADV_DONTNEED` by default, or resets with `MADV_FREE` if `MIMALLOC_PURGE_DECOMMITS=0`.
- tcmalloc: `ReleaseMemoryToSystem` on demand, or a background thread running `ProcessBackgroundActions` that releases from the page heap at the configured release rate.

tcmalloc's tuning guide lists the cost of releasing aggressively: memory released and then needed again must be faulted back in, and releasing at small granularity breaks up hugepages, raising TLB misses. That is exactly why Temeraire releases whole hugepages.

blocks.code:
# jemalloc: options are a comma-separated list of option:value pairs
MALLOC_CONF="background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:5000,narenas:8" ./server

# mimalloc: dynamic override plus environment options
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/libmimalloc.so MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY=250 MIMALLOC_SHOW_STATS=1 ./server

# tcmalloc: linked at build time (the malloc attribute of a Bazel binary);
# release rate and per-CPU cache size are set via tcmalloc::MallocExtension
blocks.caption: How each allocator is configured. jemalloc reads MALLOC_CONF at startup; mimalloc reads MIMALLOC_ environment variables.

blocks.prompt: You switch a 64-CPU service from 64 worker threads to 1,000 threads mostly blocked on I/O, all using jemalloc with default settings. What happens to the arenas and to cached memory?
blocks.reveal: narenas defaults to 4 x 64 = 256 arenas, so after the first 256 threads each new thread shares an arena with the least load: about 4 threads per arena. Contention stays low because most threads are idle. The bigger cost is that every thread that has allocated has its own tcache, so idle threads hold cached objects. jemalloc's incremental tcache GC trims bins over time, but per-thread caching still scales with thread count. That is the problem tcmalloc's per-CPU mode was built for.

blocks.md: Published benchmarks (including those in mimalloc's README and report) measure specific workloads. Allocator rankings change with object sizes, thread counts and cross-thread patterns. Measure throughput, p99 latency and RSS on your own service, with production-like load, before and after switching.

Choose by the hard constraint. Many threads and a tight memory budget favour per-CPU caching (tcmalloc). Heavy cross-thread freeing and allocation-heavy runtimes suit mimalloc's per-page lists. Fine-grained control over arenas, decay and introspection (`mallctl`, stats) is jemalloc's strength. Then tune the return-to-OS delay against page-fault cost.

blocks.question: A latency-sensitive service shows p99 spikes every few seconds, and a profile shows time in page faults right after memory was purged. Which change targets this most directly?
options: Increase the number of size classes
Disable the thread cache
Lengthen the purge delay (jemalloc dirty_decay_ms or MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY) so freed pages stay mapped longer between bursts
Lower jemalloc's opt.narenas to 1
blocks.explain: The spikes come from returning pages to the OS and faulting them back in. A longer delay keeps them resident across bursts, at the cost of higher RSS. Disabling caches or arenas adds contention without fixing the faults.

blocks.question: Which statement about cross-thread frees is correct?
options: mimalloc takes the owning thread's heap lock on every remote free
jemalloc returns a remotely freed object straight to its slab with no lock
All three forbid freeing memory allocated by another thread
tcmalloc's transfer cache lets objects freed on one CPU refill another CPU's cache without going through spans
blocks.explain: tcmalloc's transfer cache is a per-size-class array of pointers that one front-end fills and another drains. mimalloc uses a lock-free CAS onto the page's thread_free list. jemalloc caches the object in the freeing thread's tcache, then locks the owner's bin when flushing.
